Dear Dr. Chalmers,

I started to use the mirt package in order to evaluate difficulty estimations of programming tasks (about a hundred) I am providing to my students (more than a hundred). I have several questions that arise mainly from the fact I am an ordinary programmer and rather incidentally approach the deep waters of statistics. I hope you'll find time to help me understand some of the following subjects.

The data contains encoded number of attempts each student needed to solve a particular assignment. The number of allowed attempts equals 3, therefore matrix contains 3, if the student solved task on the first attempt, 2 - second attempt, 1 - third. 0 - failed to solve the task on any of the attempts. NA - if there was no attempt on the task by the user.

Example data:

ID01 ID02 ID03 ...
3    1    0    ...
NA   NA   0    ...
2    NA   NA   ...
...  ...  ...

This is the format I use for the graded response model.

Q1. The first question is: what will be the valid format to encode data for the sequential response model?

The next problem I face is lots of NA's. There are very few students that attempted to solve all tasks. Most of them solved not more than about a half of tasks. I am unable to evaluate goodness of fit for this model with any of the methods provided in mirt package, as the data contains too much NA's.

Q2. Is there any way of calculating goodness of fit in such situation?

Any help from you will be appreciated.

Thank you very much for the great piece of work you provide to the R community.

Best Regards
Maciek

messages.subject_clean: multidimensional Rasch/PCM model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jing,

There's several ways to do this, though perhaps the easiest is just to specify a mirt.model() definition and apply some equality constraints. For example, a multidimensional Rasch model could be expressed as

model <- " F1 = 1-5
                 F2 = 6-10
                COV = F1*F2
                CONSTRAIN = (1-5, a1), (6-10, a2)"

mod <- mirt(data, model)

Rasch models are really just slope constrained 2PL models, so for multidimensional extensions you only need to constrain the slopes to be equal within each respective dimension. HTH.

Phil

> > I already previously ran the M2(na.rm = TRUE) function, however it confused me, as results I received were:
>
> GRM: M2: 2122,825, df: 2622, p: 1, RMSEA: 0, RMSEA_5: 0, RMSEA_95: 0, SRMSR: 0,2606455, TLI: 2.516962, CFI: 1
> Sequential: M2: 2093,157, df: 2622, p: 1, RMSEA: 0, RMSEA_5: 0, RMSEA_95: 0, SRMSR: 0,259721, TLI: 2.607798, CFI: 1
>
> In my dataset there are about 300 rows (participants) and only 15 made attempts to solve all tasks. All other 284 rows contain NA's. Could you please clarify, how reliable are these results? Shouldn't I doubt when I see these sharp values of p = 1 and CFI = 1?

You have good intuition, I too doubt the veracity of these results given only 15 full response vectors. At best these are tentative results that have not rejected the null of 'good fit', but given the data used this is probably very under powered. I don't think a theoretical solution for the M2 statistic with so much missing data has appeared in the literature yet, so at this point you may be stuck with only there conservative results.

Phil

Hi Phil, the first warning I just ignored because I am trying to use your method of DIF detection. So I only ran the multiGroup model without freeing the latent mean/variance (and without anchor items) to identify anchors using this code:

>
That's good to know the 0x0 df output means no DIF (based on criterion set). I'm wondering though if everything looks okay to you in the code above? When I run the code above, I am able to detect DIF in my mod2/dif2 models. But I always get the 0x0 df output in the mod1/dif1 models, no matter what criterion I set in the dif1 seq_stat (e.g., I even set the seq_stat to a super low bar of .80 and removed the BH adjustment and the 0x0 df output still resulted...Since I'm detecting DIF in mod2/dif2, I wasn't sure if it makes sense that I'm not detecting DIF in mod1/dif1 (which is only being run for the purposes of selecting an anchor anyway)? Or perhaps I am doing something wrong..?

Thank you for your time,
J

messages.body_plain:
Yes, everything in your code looks fine, but again I think the best practice is to use anchor items first. The process described in the DTF paper isn't completely kosher, but then interest was less about DIF and more about the aggregate DTF effects. For DTF, even if the wrong anchor items are chosen (and therefore alternative items end up showing DIF) the composite still should show response bias in the test as a whole.

Regarding the output from the DIF() function, I recall that there was some weird bug that appears on the current CRAN version that has been patched on the Github dev. Feel free to install that first and check again, though I am planning on releasing a new version of mirt next week. Cheers.

Phil

On Wed, Sep 11, 2019 at 2:05 PM Ed Merkle <ecme...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Phil,
>
> I am interested in the use of priors on item parameters, as could be done via the mirt parprior argument.

That input argument is a little dated at this point, but still works fine. You may prefer the syntax approach with the PRIOR keyword instead.

>
> It seems like these priors are often added to improve model convergence (like in a 3pl), but then we ignore the priors and treat the estimated model parameters as if they were maximum likelihood estimates. Would you agree?

Perhaps historically this may have been true, but in (hopefully most) modern IRT software the prior information is included when computing the ACOV, so the standard errors (or rather, the posterior standard deviations) are reported instead. You could estimate the SEs via ML in mirt, but you'd have to first fit the model to obtain the MAP estimates and then fit a new model using these values as "estimated" but have the model converge instantly (e.g., by passing TOL = NaN).

>
> I know some papers by Swaminathan in the 1980s that seem to motivate this approach, but I'm wondering whether you know of others. I am mostly interested in how this practice came to be.

I imagine it was due to software support at the time. Old programs like TESTFACT and MULTILOG often took different approaches to compute the ACOV, some of which did not include the prior parameter distribution information directly in the calculations. I think that's bad practice these days though, particularly given recent advancements in obtaining the ACOV/posterior covariance matrix (PCOV? I'm not sure there's a formal name for this mathematical object....) when fitting models via the EM algorithm. HTH.

messages.body_plain:
Please use the mirt-package google forum for questions like these in the future. I've forwarded this question to the forum for others to benefit from as well.

The RSM is just a special case of the GPCM when all a1 parameters are equal (or equivalently set to 1 and the latent variance term is something other than 1), though it's often specified with thresholds rather than intercepts. Below is an example of transforming thresholds to intercept parameters via traditional2mirt() and simulating the data that way. Just modify the following example and replace the values as you need:

#make some data
set.seed(1234)
a <- matrix(1, 10)
b <- matrix(c(-1.5, 0, 1.5), 10, 3, byrow = TRUE)
c <- seq(0, 2, length.out=10)
bprime <- b + c
si <- t(apply(bprime, 1,
      function(x) traditional2mirt(x = c(a=1, b=x), 'gpcm', ncat=4)))
data <- simdata(si[,1], si[,6:9], 2000, itemtype = rep('gpcm',10))

mod1 <- mirt(data, 1, 'Rasch')
coef(mod1, simplify=TRUE, IRTpars=TRUE) # compare to bprime
mod2 <- mirt(data, 1, itemtype = 'rsm')
coef(mod2, simplify=TRUE)
anova(mod2, mod1) #not sig, mod2 should be preferred
itemplot(mod2, 1)
itemplot(mod2, 10)

Phil

Thanks in advance

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel,

This is a confusing topic, so now would probably be a good time to discuss the issue. To answer your questions; no, the current approach is likely not what you want to ensure each session gets it's own session name (see the createSessionName() function for a better alternative). The better flow would be something more akin to :

mysession<-createSessionName()
mirtCAT_preable( ...,sessionName=mysession,...)
createShinyGUI(mysession, ...)

or what the current dev version of the package does (which is better yet)

mysession<-paste0(createSessionName(), Sys.time())
mirtCAT_preable( ...,sessionName=mysession,...)
createShinyGUI(mysession, ...)

The idea here is that each time a user logs into the server the uploaded server.R/ui.R files are effectively re-sourced into an R session, so in your example code everyone would get the same session name. This is bad, because if there are two instances of users logged in at the same time then the answers of one user actually influence the session of the other user since they are being written to the same isolated enviroment. Since I added the sessionName input this is avoided so long as a sufficiently random session name is provided to each user, which in the current CRAN version is a randomly generated character vector with 30 upper/lower cases (hence, the odds that any two session would ever share at the exact moment is extremely small). The dev version even goes one step further now to paste on the date/time the session started, so its now astronomically unlikely for two users to share the same session name simultaneously.

The described problem is a limitation with the free version of shiny server, but this is a reasonably clever hack to avoid problems and allow single servers to be overloaded (the better solution would be to force individuals onto separate servers at the outset with the pro versions of shiny, or to create some type of virtual drives on the server to mimic the same behaviour). HTH with the understanding.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: Itemfit: Rows in supplied and starting value data.frame objects do not match
messages.body_plain:
Hi Maciek,

This largely has to do with the fact that your sample size is quite small (less than N=111 after removing empty rows) and the items have several options (some as high as 9 unique observations; use apply(data_tasks, 2, table)). This makes the data counts very sparse, which is what caused the problem you reported last time. It might be a better strategy to collapse categories that are sparse (if theoretically  justifiable), or otherwise abandon these itemfit statistics since they will be very under-powered anyway.

Regarding the parametric bootstrap, because many of your cell counts were 1-2 in a good number of items the IRT intercept parameters are fairly extreme, so generating data where these observations are realized in a new random sample is unlikely. Hence, the data fails to create a reasonably close new sample with the same pattern of missingness 100x in a row. I think the scenario is just too extreme to work with here for these simulation fit statistics. You might have better luck when using alternatives? It's difficult to tell, but either way detecting misfit is going to be quite difficult given the effective sample size.

Phil

messages.subject: Problem in Constraining Covariance between Groups in multi-dimensional Multi-group model
messages.subject_clean: Problem in Constraining Covariance between Groups in multi-dimensional Multi-group model
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have an analysis where I have reason to believe that nature of the latent variable underlying some items is changing as the result of an intervention.  I've setup an analysis that uses pre-/post- intervention groups with items from the focal scale and a secondary scale that should be correlated to focal scale, but unaffected by intervention. I'm trying to test if the correlation between the focal scale and secondary scale shifts as the result of the intervention (along with more typical DIF measures) by comparing a model with free covariances across groups to a model with covariances constrained to be equal across groups.

I seem to be unable to constrain the covariance between two latent factors to be equal across groups.  Code below shows issue with output inline and commented out.  Note that removing the line "CONSTRAINB = (GROUP, COV_21)" lets model run fine, but with different covariances across group.  I'm not sure if this is problem of me conceptualizing analysis or an error in MIRT so I am posting here first before github.  I have also tried using the constrain parameter and it gives same error.  Adding invariance terms "free_vars" frees the variances across groups, but also restricts the covariances to be equal across groups, not including it constrains variances and frees the covariances.  I seem to be able to constrain or free either the variances or the covariances across groups through various methods, but never both.

In code below, I've fixed some slopes to 1 because of comments here (https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/mirt-package/CONSTRAIN$20covariance|sort:date/mirt-package/Brrlg6YRvns/LiEHeJJGAwAJ <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/mirt-package/CONSTRAIN$20covariance%7Csort:date/mirt-package/Brrlg6YRvns/LiEHeJJGAwAJ>), but I don't think this should be necessary since constraining reference group latent variances to 1 should cause no trouble with my analyses...  I've also constrained all items to be invariant across groups for simplicity, but I believe that allowing some items (but not all) to vary across groups should be identified.

```
#make some Graded response data - issue isn't with data so I simply create same item over and over
set.seed(1234)
Group<-sample(c("a","b"),2000,replace=T)
a <- matrix(rep(1, 10))
d <- matrix(c(1,0.5,-.5,-1), 10, 4, byrow = TRUE)
c <- seq(-1, 1, length.out=10)
data <- simdata(a, d, 2000, itemtype = rep('graded',10))

# Setup model then run with commented out error
MM <- mirt.model("
 F1=1-5
 F2=6-10
 COV  = F1*F2
 CONSTRAINB = (2-5,a1),(7-10,a2),(1-10,d1),(1-10,d2),(1-10,d3),(1-10,d4)
 CONSTRAINB = (GROUP, COV_21)
 FIXED = (GROUP, MEAN_1  ),(GROUP, MEAN_2  ),(GROUP, COV_11  ),(GROUP, COV_22  ), (1,a1),(6,a2)
 START = (GROUP, MEAN_1,0),(GROUP, MEAN_2,0),(GROUP, COV_11,1),(GROUP, COV_22,1), (1,a1,1),(6,a2,1)
 ", itemnames=select(tmpdat.1,-GroupExp))
multipleGroup(data,MM,tol=NA,group=Group,method="MHRM")
##   Error in UpdateConstrain(pars = pars, constrain = constrain, invariance = invariance,  :
##     trying to get slot "parnum" from an object of a basic class ("NULL") with no slots
##   In addition: Warning message:
##   In UpdateConstrain(pars = pars, constrain = constrain, invariance = invariance,  :
##     NAs introduced by coercion

# Run same model on same data with no restrictions to covariance and it seems fine
 MM <- mirt.model("
 F1=1-5
 F2=6-10
 COV  = F1*F2
 CONSTRAINB = (2-5,a1),(7-10,a2),(1-10,d1),(1-10,d2),(1-10,d3),(1-10,d4)

 FIXED = (GROUP, MEAN_1  ),(GROUP, MEAN_2  ),(GROUP, COV_11  ),(GROUP, COV_22  ), (1,a1),(6,a2)
 START = (GROUP, MEAN_1,0),(GROUP, MEAN_2,0),(GROUP, COV_11,1),(GROUP, COV_22,1), (1,a1,1),(6,a2,1)
 ", itemnames=select(tmpdat.1,-GroupExp))
multipleGroup(data,MM,tol=NA,group=Group,method="MHRM")
##   Stage 3 = 35, LL = -30973.8, AR(0.50) = [0.31; 0.30], gam = 0.0126, Max-Change = 0.0007
##
##   Calculating log-likelihood...
##
##   Call:
##   multipleGroup(data = data, model = MM, group = Group, method = "MHRM",
##   ##       tol = NA)
##
##   ##   Full-information item factor analysis with 2 factor(s).
##   Converged within 0.001 tolerance after 35 MHRM iterations.
##   mirt version: 1.30.10
##   ##   M-step optimizer: NR1
##   Latent density type: Gaussian
##
##   Log-likelihood = -28744, SE = 0.105
##   Estimated parameters: 98
##   AIC = 57588; AICc = 57591
##   BIC = 57868; SABIC = 57709
##   G2 (9765574) = 29931, p = 1
##   RMSEA = 0, CFI = NaN, TLI = NaN
```

Dear Phil
I think you have some examples in mirt manual for the first four cases. hear is some briefly definition from appendix c of attached article:

1- Conﬁgural Invariance=no constrain or as you called it separate analysis for each group

2- Weak Invariance= metric invaraince= Constrain item slopes equal across groups

3- Strong Invariance= scalar invaraince=Constrain item intercepts and slopes equal across groups

4- Strict Invariance=in addition to items' slopes and intercepts constrain item residual variances to be equal across groups,

5- Invariance of the Factor Variance-Covariance Matrixes=in addition to items' slopes, intercepts and residual constrain  factor variances and covariances to be equal across groups. it is also informative to test whether the full variance/covariance matrix is also invariant across groups. This is done by adding equality constraints on the factor covariances and by fixing all factor variances to one in all groups.

6- Latent Mean Invariance=factor means were constrained to equality across groups (i.e., fixed to zero in all groups).

Phil
